Skip next section German economic institutes raise growth forecasts 09/03/2026 September 3, 2026 German economic institutes raise growth forecasts Germany's RWI and Ifo economic institutes have lifted growth forecasts for the German economy, citing stronger fiscal spending and exports. In its latest assessment, the RWI said Germany's economy will grow by 1.3% in 2026, a sharp upward revision from the 0.8% growth predicted in June. The Ifo said German gross domestic product (GDP) is expected to grow by 1.4% in 2026 and 1.2% in 2027, both up from previous estimates of 0.8%. According to the Ifo's assessment , the German federal government's debt-financed investment package and increased demand from abroad are contributing to this positive trend. The Munich-based institute said that government spending on infrastructure, climate neutrality and defence provided fiscal stimulus worth €40 billion ($46.36 billion), or 0.8% ​of GDP, in 2026. Both institutes assessed that fiscal spending and exports have been able to outweigh the drag from higher energy prices. However, RWI cautioned that this export momentum would likely fade later this year because the recent gains were a temporary effect of the rebound from disruptions related to US tariffs last year. Additionally, the RWI said high ​energy prices, bureaucracy and weak competitiveness continue to weigh on investment. This comes along with severe weaknesses in Germany's critical automotive industry, which is hemorrhaging jobs and closing factories . "Of course they will be closed after our cultural center was expelled from there [from Berlin]," Lavrov said, speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok. "They deliberately took this step — they could not have failed to understand — which means the end of their cultural presence in Russia," Lavrov said, according to state news agency TASS. The comes after Germany blamed Russia for an attempted ‌drone ⁠attack at ⁠the Leipzig/Halle Airport. Germany's response to that incident included closing the Russian House cultural center in Berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn. Goethe operates in around 100 countries worldwide, promoting the study of the German language and providing information about German culture and society. Russia's first Goethe-Institut opened in Moscow in 1992, shortly after the collapse of the Soviet Union. The Goethe-Institut is one of the last German institutions still operating in Russia. Investigators are looking into a possible political motive, an LKA spokesperson said. The spokesperson did not immediately identify the company involved. However, the Bild tabloid reported that the fire was set at a construction site near the headquarters of Rohde & Schwarz, a technology company that produces communication systems for the Bundeswehr, among other things. A spokesperson for the company confirmed the police and fire department response, emphasizing, however, "our company premises themselves are not affected," local public broadcaster BR reported. Police said multiple incendiary devices were thrown from a vehicle at the construction site in Munich's Berg am Laim neighborhood early Thursday morning around midnight. According to the LKA, various defense contractors are based in the nearby building complex. At least one of the incendiary devices sparked a fire that police officers extinguished. Despite the fire, no major damage was caused, a Munich police spokesperson said. However, another incendiary device had to be defused by special forces. Following a short manhunt, a 28-year-old woman and a 38-year-old man, both Bulgarian citizens, according to BR, were arrested at a nearby gas station, and were being questioned Thursday. Photograph: Caitlin Ochs/Reuters US immigration Supreme court to hear case challenging Trump’s immigration detention policy Court will review practice of indefinite detention for undocumented immigrants living in the US Ariana Baio Thu 1 Oct 2026 16.20 EDT Last modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 16.42 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The US supreme court agreed on Thursday to take up a case challenging the Trump administration’s practice of indefinite detention for undocumented immigrants living in the US and awaiting deportation proceedings. At the center of the immigration case is a dispute over Donald Trump’s reinterpretation of a longstanding policy that has led to a huge surge in the number of migrants held in detention centers . For years, undocumented immigrants, who had been living in the US could be released back into their communities on bond, so long as they did not pose a threat to safety or were considered a flight risk. But last year, administration officials reinterpreted the statute to mean any migrant who entered the US illegally should be held in detention while awaiting legal proceedings. The case was the latest Trump-era immigration policy to be added to the high court’s docket this term. This week, justices said they would hear arguments in a case challenging the administration’s “third-country” deportations , which allow immigrants to be sent to a country other than their own. The challenger to the Trump administration’s reinterpreted policy denying bond hearings is Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a Brazilian citizen who has been living in the US for more than 20 years. Authorities say Barbosa da Cunha entered the US illegally in or around 2005. He owns a home in Massachusetts, runs a small construction company, has a wife and two US-born children, and has never been charged with a crime. He was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents last year while driving to work and moved to an immigration detention facility in Buffalo, New York. Barbosa da Cunha had requested a bond hearing but was denied. A district court sided with Barbosa da Cunha, ordering the government to give him a bond hearing. An appeals court affirmed that decision after the administration appealed. But now lawyers for the government are asking the supreme court to intervene. The dispute is not unique to Barbosa da Cunha; lower courts have been split on the Trump administration’s policy reinterpretation in other immigration cases as well. More than 500 district court judges and nine of the 11 federal appeals courts who have heard similar cases have rejected the Trump administration’s new interpretation, according to the New York Times. Judges have largely agreed that the statute the Trump administration is using to indefinitely detain undocumented immigrants only applies to those who have been apprehended at a port of entry, such as the US-Mexico border. https://www.politico.eu/article/poland-s.text: Poland's defense minister said Tuesday that the Pentagon had given a “green light” to plans for a permanent U.S. military base in the country, with President Donald Trump expected to make a final decision in early December. Speaking after talks with U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in Washington, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said his American counterpart told him that “everything is moving in the right direction.” “We interpret that as a green light from the Pentagon,” he said. The project has not yet received formal U.S. approval. Advertisement Advertisement The Pentagon’s own account stopped short of endorsing the base or confirming the December timetable, but acknowledged ongoing talks about strengthening the permanent U.S. military presence in Poland. Hegseth praised Poland’s military buildup, calling its army “one of the most formidable” in Europe. He also pushed for European NATO allies to take greater responsibility for their own defense, potentially allowing Washington to reduce its troop presence on the continent. Poland already hosts thousands of American troops, largely on rotating deployments. But Warsaw is pushing for a permanent base as the Pentagon reviews its military presence across Europe, with other NATO allies fearing Trump could withdraw thousands more troops . The review is expected to conclude by December. The project is also a rare point of agreement between Poland's feuding leaders. Prime Minister Donald Tusk and President Karol Nawrocki — a Trump ally whom the U.S. president backed in last year's election — agreed last week to cooperate on securing the base, despite their bitter confrontation over control of Poland's top court. Nawrocki has embraced the proposed name “Fort Trump,” first floated by his predecessor, Andrzej Duda, in 2018. The U.S. Department of Defense didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
